assessed
  • asymmetry — The evidence_summary.json measured fields for the newsletter popup accept/reject pair show a clear imbalance: area_ratio 2.5 (accept button occupies 2.5x the area of the reject option), contrast_ratio 4.12 (accept has much higher contrast/prominence than reject), font_size_ratio 1.17, and a vertical_position_delta_px of -52 (accept sits above reject, the more favorable position), plus a negative tab_order_delta indicating the accept option is reached first in tab order. These are multiple independent axes (area, contrast, font size, position, tab order) all skewed in favor of "Yes, sign me up" over "No thanks, I don't like saving money" — the negative option's copy itself ("I don't like saving money") is also a guilt-trip framing typical of confirmshaming, which reinforces that the visual asymmetry is intentional rather than incidental styling. The combination of a 2.5x area ratio and >4:1 contrast ratio between the two opposing choices exceeds what would be expected from ordinary UI styling variance and reads as a deliberate design choice to steer the user toward opting in. This matches the code agent's "approached threshold" finding but the multi-axis convergence (area + contrast + position + tab order all pointing the same direction) pushes this past "unsure" into "fires" territory, albeit at moderate rather than extreme severity since it's a single popup interaction rather than a checkout-critical asymmetry.
  • covertness — The negative option in the newsletter modal is not merely visually de-emphasized (smaller/lower contrast) but is worded as "No thanks, I don't like saving money" — a confrontational, guilt-inducing label that misrepresents what declining actually does (it doesn't cost the user money, it just opts out of a mailing list). This kind of "confirmshaming" phrasing is a classic technique for concealing the true, simple action ("decline the popup") behind loaded language designed to make users hesitate or feel foolish for choosing it, rather than a neutral/coincidental label like "No thanks" or "Not now" (which is what appears in the later step_002 notification popup, "Not now" vs "Enable" — a much more neutral, non-covert pairing by contrast). The evidence_summary's visual_asymmetry entry confirms the negative option also has lower contrast, smaller font, and reversed tab order compared to the accept button, compounding the disguising effect: the option is both textually manipulated and visually suppressed, suggesting deliberate design intent to discourage/hide the true decline action rather than an incidental layout choice. However, this is a single-instance textual/visual pattern from one modal, and other similar modals (step_002's notification prompt) use much more neutral opt-out language, suggesting the covert design was a specific, deliberate choice for this particular popup rather than a site-wide accident. I did not find additional corroborating instances of hidden/disguised reject controls elsewhere in the flow (e.g., cancellation, cart opt-outs use a plain checkbox "Keep plan" rather than disguised text), which keeps severity moderate and confidence not fully certain.
  • information_hiding — The evidence_summary.json price_drift data shows two mid-checkout increases explicitly labeled "(new)" in the UI copy itself: a ₹149 "Payment processing fee (new)" that first appears at step 14 (Payment details page) and a ₹199 "Service & handling fee (new)" that first appears at step 17 (Review page, immediately before "Place order"). Neither fee was mentioned on the product page (steps 5-9), during Add to Cart, or on the Shipping step (step 13), where the running total was still shown as ₹4,898 with no indication that further mandatory charges were coming. These are not user-caused increases (no quantity change, no optional add-on selected by the user at that point) — they are mandatory fees for completing the purchase that were withheld until the user was already deep in the checkout funnel, which matches the classic "drip pricing" information-hiding pattern. Additionally, the cart step (step 10) shows a "Auralis Protection Plan+ (auto-added)" line item with a pre-checked "Keep plan" checkbox — an added cost the user did not proactively choose, appearing without prior warning on the product page. Combined, this constitutes withholding cost information until late in the flow. Severity is high (4/5) because the fees are labeled "(new)" and appear only at the two final steps of a purchase-cheapest goal, directly increasing the total the user must pay by ~₹347 beyond what was shown throughout most of the shopping/cart process, and it happens twice in the same flow (payment step, then review step), compounding the surprise.
  • complexity — The code agent flagged only one dimension (total_actions_required=18) as exceeding the purchase_cheapest baseline, with moderate confidence (0.75). Reviewing the step sequence, a meaningful portion of the 18 actions are not inherent to a simple "find and buy cheapest item" flow: step 2 dismisses a newsletter popup, step 3 dismisses a "nagging modal," and step 11 dismisses another nagging modal that reappeared after step 9/10 cart navigation clicks (steps 9 and 10 both target the same cart-icon selector, suggesting a repeated/interrupted click). This pattern of repeated interstitials and redundant clicks does inflate the action count beyond what would be inherent to checkout (browse->product->add to cart->checkout->shipping->payment->review->confirm is roughly 8-10 steps), but it's hard to cleanly separate "inherent" steps from "friction" steps using only the aggregate total_actions_required metric, and the checkout flow itself (shipping/payment/review, 3 steps) is standard e-commerce and not excessive. The option_counts (12-18 UI elements visible per page, mostly nav links, cards, footer) look like normal page furniture, not an overloaded decision point — screenshots show simple product grids and short checkout forms with only 2-4 form fields per page, no unusually large fields or menus. Reading grade (10.8-11.3) is moderately high but not extreme, and only measured on early marketing pages, not on any consent/cancellation copy. Given the code agent's single flagged dimension is plausible but the qualitative flow doesn't show an overloaded decision point or exceptionally complex language, and the extra actions seem more attributable to nagging/interruption patterns (a different attribute) rather than true "complexity" overload, I lean unsure rather than a clear fires or no.
